lastText: GHQSITUATION REPORTHome1914191519161917191811 November 1918The Hundred DaysThe armistice comes into force at eleven in the morning. The British armies, which began the year holding the longest line in France and short of men, have ended it advancing on a broad front, with a large share of the prisoners and guns taken since August to their credit. The army that landed in August 1914 has been replaced several times over, and the Cabinet that sent it has been replaced twice. The argument between the generals and the politicians is not over, and will be carried on in print for the next twenty years.The front · 11 November 1918Expand the mapLoosParisSaint-OmerMontreuilCalaisDoullensLondon-8MANPOWER -2MUNITIONS -3POLITICAL CAPITAL Settled recordLanding, August 1914: assembled at Maubeuge. The Seine, September 1914: the army kept to the line. Ypres, 1914: the line was held. The Dardanelles, March 1915: the 29th Division released. The shortage of shells: told to the press. Loos: the ground was refused. Gallipoli, November 1915: Anzac and Suvla evacuated, Helles held. December 1915: Haig appointed. 1916: compulsion for all men at once. The Somme: a compromise plan, and a costly first day. The tanks: a dozen used on 15 September, the rest held. Calais, February 1917: accepted under protest. Convoy: tried from May 1917.
